title: 28 Vallejo St Residence Entry
description: Design by David Feix.  The entry  portal and walls along the street were necessary to give privacy at the front of the house, especially since passersby would be looking directly down into the ground floor windows from the street.  The walls accomplish both screening for privacy  and give a sense of mystery of what lies beyond.  The entry gate is a custom steel gate with inset etched glass block, and matches the detail of the entry door at the house.  The entry portal matches the raised cube over the stair well at the entry to the house, which is just visible at the top of the photo, and washes the entire house with natural light.

title: View back towards jacuzzi and Heliconias
description: This shot shows many succulents from around the world; Aeoniums from the Canary Islands, Echeverias and Sedum palmeri, Heliconia schiedeana and Brahea 'Clara' from Mexico, Bromeliads such as Dyckias, Porteas, Aechmeas, Neoregelias and Salvia splendens 'Vanhouttii' from Brazil, and Restios from South Africa.  Las unicas plantas nativas de California en esta foto son el Roble, Quercus agrifolia, and los Redwoods, Sequoia sempervirens del vicino por tras del muro.

title: Stairs down to the garden below
28 Vallejo St Entry Courtyard Garden
description: View down from second story bathroom window  of entry porch porch and bench at walk with massed pots of Farfugium japonicum 'aurea maculata' and Chamaedorea tepejilote palm, and various other bromeliads and ferns below.  This area is deeply shaded by an overhead Coast Live Oak tree that was the only remaining tree from the garden prior to the home and landscape remodeling.

title: Central raised planter at main terrace
Neoregelias, Billbergia vittata and Uncinia uncinata
description: A combination of bromeliads and a colorful bronzy New Zealand sedge relative as ground cover around a Balinese stone carved lantern with low voltage lighting.

title: 28 Vallejo St Garden, Entry view at gate
description: This is the view towards the front porch as seen upon opening the gate at the pergola.  The front courtyard is just off to the right in this view, and the entry walk is shaded by a Coast Live Oak that was original to the garden before the remodel.  More palms were used to line both sides of the walk, including more potted Chamaedorea microspadix, Chamaedorea tepejilote on the right, another Trachycarpus fortunei, and understory Neoregelia bromeliads.

title: Accent pots and plantings at terrace
28 Vallejo St Residence,  Berkeley Hills
description: Design by David Feix.  Inside view of secluded front courtyard garden showing how the terrace is below street level, yet still open, airy and full of light for lower level rooms.  The plantings are still very young in this shot, less than 6 months after initial planting.  Variegated foliage was selected to give additional year round interest in this narrow, north side entry garden, which primarily acts as a viewing garden from the below grade first floor at the house, which puts the plantings right at window level.  The Windmill Palm, Trachycarpus fortunei was stripped of the old leaf bases, revealing the wonderfully colorful striped trunk with shades of blue and green that match the color of the roof eaves.  The stepped walls and paving details, and surrounding walls are meant to engage with the house, as well as bounce light back into the below grade bedroom and bath, all within a 15 foot deep front yard setback..

title: 28 Vallejo St Garden plantings upon entry
description: View of side yard plantings at entry walk, as seen from entering gate.  The bromeliads in the foreground are Neoregelias, which turn purple at the center in this case, combines with some Carex morrowii 'Evergold' as edging, along with Blechnum gibbum and Chamaedorea tepejilote, several Daphe odora marginata, and an Edgeworth chrysantha all leafed out and looking tropical.  The Live Oak tree trunk is set between a break in the wall, so we could keep the tree, which shades the whole entry way.

title: Banksia blechnifolia and Linaria reticulata
description: Close-up shot of fern-like foliage,(Blechnum is a fern genus), but I don't have the right lens to really show the detail of the foliage.  New growth is fuzzy and apricot orange, before it settles into mature form with glossy deep green leaves.  This plant also has a very interesting habit of snaking out stems that follow the ground, and will form an extensive ground cover if allowed to do its thing.  The stems are also strangely fuzzy, and look like alien invaders.

title: Looking down on colorful bromeliads in pot
28 Vallejo St Rear Garden
description: View looking down upon rear terrace off family room, curving stairs down to rear garden, glimpse of kitchen cantilevered deck and jacuzzi below.

title: Table and planters at main terrace below oak canopy
Succulents for dappled sun below a Coast Live Oak
description: In this summer photographed vignette, I eventually discovered that the Arctotis 'Purple Torch' wasn't going to get enough sun to remain healthy and vigorously compact, and had already started to smother surrounding plants.  Much better to give it full sun in the first place, rather than try to force it to work as i wanted it to. At the opposite extreme, the Hawaiian tree ferns, Cibotium glaucum which I placed behind this viewpoint in the garden didn't deal well with the September/October heat waves and a two hour blast of direct late afternoon sun it got, and I had to pull them out of the garden as they were just getting smaller and smaller by the month.  The main players in this scene ended up being the most reliable, which is one reason I use them so frequently in my garden designs.  Hurray for Aeonium canariense, Sedum palmeri, Echeveria elegans and various bromeliads such as these Dyckia 'Cactus Ranch Red' and Portea 'Jungles'. The Brahea 'Clara' is a fabulous accent foliage palm for SF Bay Area gardens as well, too little planted around town as it ought to be...

title: 28 Vallejo St Kitchen interior
description: Design by Mario Trejo of Trejo Designs, (510 418 0823)

title: Portea 'Jungles' at 28 Vallejo St Garden
description: Vignette with Aeonium canariensis subplanum and Portea 'Jungles' with bronze-red-purplish foliage and brilliantly blue colored berries on very long lasting spikes, set below arching silver foliaged Brahea 'Clara' palm.  The fence/wall beyond at the rear property line was designed to alternate between horizontal planes of ipe wood planks and blinding white stucco, to give further visual interest and interplay in the garden.

title: 28 Vallejo St Entry Courtyard Garden
description: Vignette showing Trachycarpus fortunei palm stripped of fiber at trunk to reveal stripes, mixed with Vriesea bromeliads and dwarf Tree Ferns-Blechnum gibbum and more Chamaedorea tepejilote palms.

title: 28 Vallejo St, View upon entering rear garden from the street
description: View across jacuzzi to rear fence/wall with specimen Brahea 'Clara' against wall and Portea 'Jungles' and Neoregelia bromeliads and succulents below palm.  The design intent of the plantings and hardscape was to create both a sheltered and private garden area while soaking in the jacuzzi, with views out into the garden, as well as create interesting patterns of hardscape and plantings as viewed from the 3 story house above.

title: Coast Live Oak tree and raised terrace
28 Vallejo St Rear Garden
description: Design by David Feix.  This vignette  is taken looking down at the rear garden from the kitchen terrace 3 stories above.  I especially like how the concrete paving has taken on an organic quality with the stain, looking like roots or water channels through a delta, and the  turquoise inset pebbles  have a meditative quality that sets me to day dreaming when I look down on this scene.  The fact that nothing is quite formally symmetrical, yet very ordered, gets to the nature of  Islamic gardens.

title: 28 Vallejo St Residence, Backyard  Garden
description: Geometry with variations on squares, and Brahea 'Clara' as star of the show.  Notice how the pendant foliage on the palm is also repeated with the pendant foliage of the Restio, Cannomois grande in the large urn.  The plantings in this back yard were intended to use foliage texture and color as the primary emphasis, with some deep red flowering accents from the Salvia splendens 'Van Houtei' and Arctotis 'Purple Torch'  and orange accents  from the blooming Dyckia bromeliads and Hedychium greenii.

title: 28 Vallejo St Front Entry Courtyard
description: Blechnum gibbum 'Silver Lady' and Trachycarpus fortunei with stripped trunk revealing shades of green and pale blue stripes.  The understory bromeliads include Nidularium innocentii in the foreground, and some Vriesea 'Hawaiian Sunset' hybrids below.

title: Rex Begonias in the shade
description: These Rex begonias aren't always the easiest type to grow here in California, as we don't really have the heat and humidity they thrive on.  On the other hand, they can make phenomenal summer annuals in bright shade out in the garden.

title: Nidularium bilbergioides
description: A bromeliad teated as an annual, as it isn't quite hardy enough to withstand the winter rains and cold, but gives great color for months at a time.

title: Middle raised planter at main terrace
Plantings at Entry Wall
description: I ended up regretting planting the Equisetum against this planter wall, wistfully thinking that a bamboo rhizome barrier would be sufficient to keep it in check.  It did behave for the first two years, but then, no surprise really, it leaped the boundary edging and started to run everywhere.  Lesson learned, don't underestimate know invasive species.

title: View of Entry Courtyard from lower bathroom
28 Vallejo St Rear Garden Main Terrace
description: Design by David Feix.  The view from the cantilevered kitchen deck down onto  the main terrace, which is at tree branches level over the garden below.  This terrace has built-in planters with their own hanging gardens, alternating with wrought iron railings.  The feeling is one of being in a tree fort, and is one of the most relaxing spaces I think I've ever had the pleasure to design.  The perfect symmetry of this terrace is interrupted by a notched corner in the foreground, where the existing oak leans into the terrace, and the walls and railings give to fit the tree.  Plantings were kept relatively restrained for me, just a few species, some big, some bold, but still with respectful deference to the oak tree canopy above.   Perhaps a contemporary take on traditional islamic garden design, or an homage to the Alhambra.
